title: multised (slim)
text: multised assembles a database of marine-sediment trace-element measurements from five external sources, harmonises them into a common schema, and progressively quality-controls the result. This site documents the slim stage: five per-source databases that share one common schema, together with the quality-control and marking work performed on them.

title: multised (slim)
text:
Pipeline generations
The data moves through four generations, each one SQLite database per source until the final merge:

pilot: each source’s raw files parsed into a per-source database whose table structure follows that source. Documented on the individual pilot sites: Mareano, Vannmiljø, ICES-DOME, MUDAB, and 4Demon.
slim (this site): every source reshaped into the same seven-table schema, then annotated with quality-control and marking flags. The underlying values are untouched; suspicious records are flagged, not deleted, so they can be reviewed.
clean: the flags are applied (uncertain rows removed), units are harmonised, and normalisation (Fe/Al) and grain-size analyses are run.
merged: the five clean databases are combined into a single database for the background / pristine-sediment analysis.

title: Fines (<63 µm)
text:
The fraction of a sediment finer than 63 µm (clay plus silt, the “mud” fraction) is a key descriptor: it governs how much surface area is available to bind trace elements, and it is the usual basis for comparing contaminant levels between samples. This page derives a single per-sample value, subsample.fines_lt63 (a percentage), from each source’s grain-size measurements, and records in fines_basis how it was obtained.
Every source with grain-size contributes (all but 4Demon, which carries no grain-size). The value is taken from the corrected standardised value value_std_corr (grain size to %), so mixed reporting units (%, g/kg) are handled uniformly and the grain-size curves repaired in the correction step (see below) are used.

title: Fines (<63 µm)
section: 1. How the fines fraction is derived
text:
1. How the fines fraction is derived
Each source encodes grain-size differently, and the parameter names do not mean the same thing across sources, so the meaning of every code was checked against the pilot parameter definitions before use.











Source
Code used
fines_lt63
fines_basis




Mareano
Clay + Silt bins
Clay (<2 µm) + Silt (2 to 63 µm)
sum_bins


Vannmiljø
FINS, complement, or clay+silt
FINS, else 100 minus GSMF_63, else GSMF2 + GSMF2_63
fins / gsmf_63_complement / clay_silt_sum


ICES-DOME
GSMF63 on a bulk matrix
Cumulative <63 µm on SEDtot, else SED2000
gsmf63_sedtot / gsmf63_sed2000


MUDAB
GSMF63 on a bulk matrix
Cumulative <63 µm on SEDtot, else SED2000
gsmf63_sedtot / gsmf63_sed2000





Two points that the derivation has to get right:

The names can be reversed. In ICES-DOME and MUDAB, GSMF63 is the mass fraction finer than 63 µm (silt and clay). In Vannmiljø the similar-looking GSMF_63 is the opposite: “Particle fraction >63 µm” (sand and coarser). So Vannmiljø’s fines come from FINS, and where only GSMF_63 exists the fines are 100 minus GSMF_63.
The fraction is relative to the matrix. A cumulative GSMF63 is the <63 µm share of whatever fraction it was measured on (see the Sample Fraction page). It is taken from the whole sample (SEDtot) first, and otherwise from SED2000 / SED1000 (the <2 mm / <1 mm material). Values measured on an already-fine fraction (which would be near 100 %) are not used. The SED2000 based values come with the gravel caveat below.







WarningThe SED2000 based fines assume negligible gravel



A SED2000 value is the <63 µm share of the <2 mm material, not of the whole sample. Converting it to a whole-sample value would need the gravel (>2 mm) proportion, but these ~2,356 subsamples (2,346 ICES-DOME, 10 MUDAB) were analysed only on the sieved <2 mm fraction, so their gravel was never measured and cannot be reconciled. They are therefore taken as whole-sample fines assuming gravel is negligible (true for open marine sediment, not for gravelly or coastal sites). They carry fines_basis = 'gsmf63_sed2000', so they can be identified, down-weighted, or dropped downstream. The gsmf63_sedtot values are genuine whole-sample fines and need no such caveat.

title: Fines (<63 µm)
text:
2. Correcting noisy grain-size curves
Much of the grain-size data outside Mareano is noisy: many curves are internally consistent (a monotone cumulative distribution) but scaled wrong, so a value that should sit near 100 % is reported as thousands of percent, with every code in the sample inflated by the same factor. A separate correction step handles this before the fines are derived, writing a corrected value (value_std_corr) and a marker (gs_corr) on each measurement:

ICES-DOME and MUDAB renormalise each over-scaled, still-monotone curve so its coarsest cutoff (the total, near the <2 mm fraction) reads 100 % (gs_corr = 'renorm'). This recovers the affected samples for the fines below.
Vannmiljø has only a handful of isolated bad values (and its codes mean “>n µm”, so the curve renormalisation does not apply): these were manually reviewed against the raw data, found incorrect, and flagged gs_corr = 'invalid' (their standardised value nulled) for removal in the clean stage.

title: Unit Conversion & Range Check
text: The five sources report the same measurements in different units: mg/kg, µg/kg, %, g/kg, and so on. Before implausible values can be flagged consistently, every value is first converted to a common unit, and the standardised chemistry values are then compared against a plausible range per element. Both are additive columns on measurement; nothing is deleted here.

title: Unit Conversion & Range Check
text:
1. Unit conversion
Each measurement gets a standardised value value_std and its unit unit_std, assigned by measurand rather than by the raw unit:

Chemistry: the 7 target elements, the Fe/Al normalisers, and organic carbon (CORG / TOC / TOC63) → mg/kg dry weight.
Grain-size composition → % (a mass/volume fraction). There is no length/µm grain-size in the data, so every grain-size value is a fraction and standardises to %.

The conversion goes through the mass fraction value / denom, where denom is “100 % of the sample mass” expressed in the original unit, then scales to the target unit’s full scale (1,000,000 for mg/kg, 100 for %).
Where a source supplies a QC-corrected value, that is the value standardised here: 4Demon’s corrected_value (which its metadata recommends for analysis) carries scale-error fixes and below-detection substitutions, while the raw value is kept as provenance. This corrected a batch of 4Demon iron values reported about 10 times too high.

title: Unit Conversion & Range Check
text:
2. Plausible range check
The standardised value_std (mg/kg) of every chemistry measurement is compared against a per-element plausible range. A value below the minimum is flagged below_min, above the maximum above_max; everything else, including grain-size (unbounded) and below-LOQ readings (a limit, not a value), stays unflagged.






Warning



These bounds are a draft, deliberately generous: they target clearly implausible values (both impossibly high and impossibly low), not strict geochemical limits, and are still to be reviewed with domain experts.

title: DB Schema (Slim)
text:
The slim schema is a common seven-table schema shared by all five sources. The core structure (table set, primary/foreign keys, and the columns needed for the trace-element analysis) is identical everywhere. Around that core, each source keeps a handful of source-specific columns that carry information only that source provides (extra identifiers, detection flags, reporting basis, and so on).
This page shows the entity-relationship diagram and, for every table, a per-source column comparison. A filled dot (●) means the column is present in that source’s slim database.

title: Harmonisation
text: Step 1 puts every source into one format, using the ICES-DOME vocabulary. Values are not changed: the original value and unit are kept, alongside a standardised value in a common unit.

title: Clean databases: overview
text:
The clean databases are the end product of the slim phase: the QC-passed, uniformly formatted databases built by applying the flags documented elsewhere on this site. This section documents how they are made. The later, separate analyses performed on the clean databases are presented on their own site.
Each source becomes one \<source\>_clean.sqlite, still per-source (a cross-source merge is a later step). The clean stage runs three steps:
Step
Does




1. Harmonise
Uniform symbols, units, depths (cm), tools, LOD/LOQ (ICES-DOME names).


2. Clean
Remove failed-QC rows; keep one of each duplicate; average technical replicates.


3. Annotate
Keep the labels; split grain-size into its own tables.

title: Common Flags
text:
After each source is reshaped into the common slim schema, a series of flagging steps annotates the data for quality control and review. Every step adds columns; it never changes or deletes a value. Suspicious or redundant records are marked so they can be inspected; the actual removal of unnecessary rows is a later Data Cleaning step, performed once the grain-size analysis is complete.
This page covers the common flags: the columns that all five sources end up with, applied the same way everywhere. The measurand classes and supporting-data availability are on the companion Class Summary page; the source-native flags that only some sources report (e.g. detection flags and outlier flags) are summarised on the Source specific page. Each section below gives a short description followed by a cross-source count table, computed directly from the current slim databases.

1. Invalid values
Adds an area_flag to site and an invalid_flag to measurement. A site is flagged outside Europe when its coordinates fall outside the European seas of interest. A measurement is flagged negative when its value is below zero, or over-range when it exceeds the physical ceiling of 100 % of the sample mass for its unit (e.g. a mg/kg value above 1,000,000). title: Source Specific
text:
Other sources
MUDAB carries native columns too (basis, matrix, qflag); its qflag and basis are already handled by the common steps, and it has no further native quality flags to fold. Its matrix is sample-fraction metadata, retained but not a src_flag.






Note



No rows have been deleted. src_flag marks source-native records for review; the actual removal happens later, when the clean databases are built.

title: Sample Fraction (matrix)
text:
Sediment can be analysed whole (a bulk grab) or after sieving to a grain-size fraction, and a trace-element value means something different depending on which. Three sources record this on each measurement in a matrix column: ICES-DOME, MUDAB, and 4Demon. Mareano and Vannmiljø have no matrix; for those the fraction has to come from the grain-size measurements themselves (a later page).
This page reads the raw matrix values, harmonises them into a common sieved/bulk class with a sieve cutoff in micrometres, and shows an important subtlety: within one sample the chemistry and the grain-size are usually measured on different fractions.

title: Sample Fraction (matrix)
text:
1. What the matrix codes mean
ICES-DOME and MUDAB use ICES MATRX codes of the form SED<mesh>, “sediment, the fraction finer than <mesh> micrometres” (SEDtot being the whole untreated sample). Meanings are from each pilot’s code_lookup table.

There is no SED64 code in any source: the fine cutoff of interest sits at 62 to 63 micrometres (SED63, SED62, FS 0-63).

title: Sample Fraction (matrix)
text:
2. Harmonised sieved / bulk class
Every measurement is placed in one of three classes from its matrix (and, for 4Demon, its fraction_range):










Class
Definition
Codes




bulk
Whole sample, or coarse sieving at or above 1000 um
SEDtot, US, SED2000, SED1000, FS 0-2000


sieved
Sieved to a fine fraction below 1000 um
SED500, SED90, SED63, SED62, SED20, FS 0-500 / 0-63 / 0-37


unspecified
No fraction stated
PK_default, missing matrix











Note



Coarse sieving to <2 mm or <1 mm (SED2000, SED1000, FS 0-2000) is the routine step that removes gravel and shell before analysis, not a fine-fraction separation, so it is counted as bulk-equivalent here rather than as a sieved fraction.

section: 5. The fraction differs between chemistry and grain-size
text:
5. The fraction differs between chemistry and grain-size
Within a single subsample the chemistry and the grain-size are usually not on the same fraction: grain-size is almost always reported on the whole sample (SEDtot), while chemistry is run on a sieved fine fraction. So there is no single “matrix per sample”; the fraction has to be read per measurement, and separately for chemistry versus grain-size.
